# VOLUME C — Logic Flows, Mathematics, Wire Formats, Operations

Companion to Volume A (system security documentation) and Volume B (API
reference). This volume contains: Part 1, machine-generated logic flows for
every function and method in the scanned tree; Part 2, the mathematics of every
algorithm with proof sketches; Part 4, the wire format catalog; Part 5, the
complete environment-variable catalog; Part 6, the complete error catalog;
Part 7, the non-technical operator manual; Part 8, test-to-tier traceability.
(There is no Part 3; the number is reserved for the formal-methods annex.)

Honesty rules (same as Volume A): generated parts cite file:line and derive
only from the parse tree; hand-authored parts distinguish standard published
results from facts about this codebase; nothing here certifies, accredits, or
classifies anything.

## Critical-path index (most security-relevant functions)

Pairwise channel: handshake and session establishment, Double Ratchet step,
frame parsing and caps, replay table. Group layer: suite pinning, commit
receive path, PQ update path, Welcome/join, KeyPackage liveness, exporter,
transcript comparison, tree cover/resolution/tree-hash. Receive sink:
filename guard, exclusive creation, reassembly, secure delete, validators.
Strategic layer: quorum bounds, ballot/equivocation handling, gateway
transfer doctrine and quarantine, active-defense loops, dual-control order
release. Platform: TPM/CNG/PKCS11 paths, PIN policy, memory wiping, ceremony
quorum, TUF dual-sign and anti-rollback. Find each by name in Part 1.

# VOLUME C, Part 2 — Mathematics with Proof Sketches

> How to read this part. Each section states (a) the mathematical construction as
> standardized, (b) the exact parameters this system uses — every size below is
> asserted live by the Known-Answer and roundtrip gates logged during test runs —
> (c) the security theorem in its standard form, and (d) a proof sketch. These are
> proof sketches of published, standard results, NOT novel proofs, and NOT proofs
> about this codebase. What the codebase proves is narrower and stronger in its own
> way: live Known-Answer Tests (KATs) and roundtrips that pin every parameter below
> to its standard vector. Section 2.13 lists precisely what is and is not proven.

## 2.1 Notation and security definitions

- `λ` denotes the security parameter. "NIST Level 5" means an attack costs at
  least as much as brute-forcing AES-256 (2^256 classical operations) or the
  equivalent quantum cost; "Level 1/3" analogously reference AES-128/192.
- A Key Encapsulation Mechanism (KEM) is a triple `(KeyGen, Encaps, Decaps)`:
  `KeyGen() -> (pk, sk)`; `Encaps(pk) -> (ct, ss)` with shared secret `ss`;
  `Decaps(sk, ct) -> ss`. Correctness: decapsulation of an honestly generated
  ciphertext returns the same `ss` except with negligible probability.
- IND-CCA2 security (the KEM gold standard): an adversary that may ask for
  decapsulations of any ciphertext except the challenge one cannot distinguish
  the real shared secret from random, except with negligible advantage.
- A signature scheme is `(KeyGen, Sign, Verify)` with the standard correctness
  condition. EUF-CMA (existential unforgeability under chosen-message attack):
  an adversary with a signing oracle cannot forge a signature on a new message.
- A hash function `H` is collision-resistant if no efficient adversary finds
  distinct `x ≠ y` with `H(x) = H(y)`; preimage-resistant if, given `H(x)` for
  random `x`, it cannot recover `x`.
- An AEAD scheme provides confidentiality (IND-CPA) plus ciphertext integrity
  (INT-CTXT): any forged ciphertext is rejected except with negligible
  probability. The standard bound degrades with the number of queries `q` and
  total data length, roughly `σ²/2^128` for 128-bit tags, where `σ` is the
  number of blocks — this is why the system caps message/table sizes (Volume A §8).
- A Key Derivation Function (KDF) takes high-entropy but non-uniform input key
  material plus context bindings and outputs pseudorandom keys. Security is
  stated in the random-oracle or PRF model: distinct contexts give independent
  keys (domain separation), which is exactly what the system's HKDF labels do.

## 2.2 Module-LWE and ML-KEM-1024 (FIPS 203)

Construction. Let `R_q = Z_q[x]/(x^256 + 1)` with `q = 3329`. ML-KEM works over
module lattices of rank `k` (`k = 4` for ML-KEM-1024). A secret vector `s` and
error vectors are sampled from a centered binomial distribution; the public key
is essentially `(A, t = A·s + e)` for a public matrix `A` derived from a seed.
Encapsulation picks fresh randomness `r`, errors `e1, e2`, computes
`(u = Aᵀ·r + e1, v = tᵀ·r + e2 + Encode(m))` for a random message `m`, and
derives the shared secret as `ss = KDF(m, H(pk))`. Decapsulation recovers `m`
by `v − sᵀ·u ≈ Encode(m)` (the errors are small, so rounding recovers `m`
exactly with overwhelming probability), then re-encrypts and checks (Fujisaki–
Okamoto transform), outputting `ss` only on match and a pseudorandom implicit-
rejection value otherwise.

Parameters used here (gated live): public key 1568 bytes, secret key 3168
bytes, ciphertext 1568 bytes, shared secret 32 bytes — the ML-KEM-1024
parameter set, NIST security Level 5.

Theorem (standard). ML-KEM is IND-CCA2 secure under the Module Learning-With-
Errors (Module-LWE) assumption for the stated rank and error distribution.

Proof sketch. In two steps. First, the underlying public-key encryption is
IND-CPA under Module-LWE: each of `(u, v)` is a fresh LWE sample, so `v`
hides `m` — replacing `t = A·s + e` by uniform (LWE step 1), then replacing
`(u, v)` by uniform (LWE step 2), leaves `m` information-theoretically hidden.
Second, the Fujisaki–Okamoto transform lifts IND-CPA to IND-CCA2 in the
(random-oracle / quantum-random-oracle) model: the re-encryption check makes
the decapsulation oracle useless, because any ciphertext the adversary submits
either decrypts to a message it already knows (it built the ciphertext) or is
rejected; the implicit-rejection value keeps even the rejection behavior from
leaking. The failure probability (decryption error per honest encapsulation,
≈ 2^-200 for the parameter set) is absorbed as a negligible term.

What this buys the system. Every pairwise handshake and every PQ ratchet step
derives forward-secret material from an IND-CCA2 KEM: even an adversary that
later steals a static secret key cannot retroactively decapsulate recorded
ciphertexts whose ephemeral randomness is gone (forward secrecy), and active
forgery of KEM ciphertexts is rejected by the FO check (this is the "fail
closed" observed in the PQ-strict abort logs).

## 2.3 Lattice signatures: ML-DSA-87 (FIPS 204)

Construction. ML-DSA is a Fiat–Shamir-with-aborts signature over module
lattices. The secret is short vectors `(s1, s2)`; the public key is
`(A, t = A·s1 + s2)` with a power-of-two modulus (`q = 8380417`) and
dimensions for parameter set 87 (`k = 8, l = 7`, hence the name). Signing
samples a masking vector `y`, computes a challenge `c = H(μ, A·y)` where `μ`
binds the message and randomness, forms candidate `z = y + c·s1`, and
*restarts* unless `z` and related hints are short enough (rejection sampling —
the "abort" loop, typically a few iterations). The signature is `(c, z, hint)`.
Verification recomputes `A·z − c·t` and checks it matches the commitment and
that all norms are within bounds.

Parameters used here (gated live): public key 2592 bytes, secret key 4896
bytes, signature 4627 bytes — the ML-DSA-87 set, NIST Level 5. Signatures in
this system bind transcripts, commits, and audit checkpoints.

Theorem (standard). ML-DSA is EUF-CMA secure under Module-LWE plus Module-SIS
(Short Integer Solution: finding a short nonzero vector in the kernel of `A`
is hard), in the (quantum) random-oracle model.

Proof sketch. The classic Fiat–Shamir argument with two modern ingredients.
First, rejection sampling makes the distribution of `z` independent of the
secret (it depends only on public parameters), so signatures leak nothing —
the abort probability is tuned so signing terminates quickly while the output
distribution is simulatable. Second, a forger that produces `(c, z)` on a new
message can be rewound (forking lemma): two valid signatures for different
challenges on the same commitment yield `A·(z − z′) = (c − c′)·t`-style
relations, i.e., a short SIS solution, or else break the underlying LWE
hiding. Hints are norm-checked precisely so this extraction goes through.

## 2.4 Hash-based signatures: SLH-DSA-256f (FIPS 205)

Construction. SLH-DSA (SPHINCS+) builds signatures purely from hash
properties: a hypertree of Merkle trees whose leaves are few-time signature
instances (FORS), each signing a message digest together with randomization.
"256f" means 256-bit security target with the "fast" (more, smaller trees)
trade-off: signing is quick, signatures are large. No lattices, no number
theory — only the hash function (SHAKE-256 here).

Parameters used here (gated live): public key 64 bytes, secret key 128 bytes,
signature 49856 bytes — SLH-DSA-SHAKE-256f. Used where long-term,
assumption-diverse anchoring matters (audit checkpoints, TUF dual-signing).

Theorem (standard). SLH-DSA is EUF-CMA secure if the underlying hash is a
pseudorandom function family with the right collision/second-preimage bounds
(the proof is in the standard model relative to stated hash properties, plus
a tight multi-target analysis).

Proof sketch. The hypertree authenticates each one-time leaf key up to the
root; FORS authenticates the message digest. A forgery must therefore either
forge a FORS signature (break the hash's subset-resilience) or substitute a
different authentication path (break Merkle collision resistance at some
tree level). Both reduce to concrete, well-studied hash properties, and the
"f" parameterization keeps the hypertree shallow enough that the reduction
loss stays within the 256-bit budget. The large signature is the price: each
of the ~d layers contributes a full authentication path.

Why two signature families. ML-DSA (fast, small) signs hot paths — commits,
transcripts, handshakes. SLH-DSA (slow-to-verify-large, but hash-only)
anchors cold trust — root checkpoints and dual-signed releases — so that a
future break in lattice assumptions alone does not quietly void recorded
history. This is assumption diversity, the same principle as the hybrid KEMs.

## 2.5 Code-based KEM: Classic McEliece-8192128f

Construction. The public key is a scrambled generator matrix of a binary
Goppa code (parameters m=13, t=128 — hence "8192 128", the "f" fast variant
uses a systematic form for quicker encapsulation). Encapsulation picks a
random error vector of exact weight `t`, computes the syndrome-like
ciphertext, and hashes the error vector to the shared secret. Decapsulation
runs the Patterson decoding algorithm with the secret Goppa polynomial to
recover the error vector, re-checks its weight, and hashes it.

Parameters used here (gated live): public key 1357824 bytes (~1.3 MB),
secret key 14120 bytes, ciphertext 208 bytes, shared secret 32 bytes.

Theorem (standard). McEliece is IND-CCA2 (after the standard randomized
padding/FO-style conversion the implementation applies) under two
assumptions: syndrome decoding of random binary linear codes is hard, and the
public scrambled matrix is indistinguishable from random (the Goppa-code
distinguisher problem).

Proof sketch. The decoding step is information-set decoding, whose cost for
`(n = 8192, t = 128)` is far above 2^256 operations classically
(`(n choose t)`-scale work with only polynomial speedups from ISD
improvements, all accounted in the parameter selection); three decades of
cryptanalysis have moved the needle by small constant factors only. The FO
layer gives CCA2 exactly as in §2.2. The cost is key size — 1.3 MB — which is
why the documentation records that full McEliece bundles cannot traverse
narrowband HF/VHF/SATCOM links and must be pre-distributed: that is physics
and arithmetic, not an implementation choice.

System role. McEliece is the conservative third leg of the hybrid combiner
(§2.7): classical X25519 (fast, small), ML-KEM-1024 (NIST primary PQC),
McEliece (non-lattice PQC). The combiner stays secure if ANY leg holds.

## 2.6 Classical leg: X25519, Ed25519, AES-256-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305, SHA-3, HKDF

X25519. Diffie–Hellman on Curve25519 (`y² = x³ + 486662x² + x` over
`2^255 − 19`), 32-byte keys. Security rests on the elliptic-curve discrete
logarithm / computational Diffie–Hellman assumption (≈128-bit classical
strength — explicitly NOT quantum-resistant, which is why it is only ever a
leg inside hybrids here, never alone on a trusted path).

Ed25519. Schnorr-type signatures on the twisted-Edwards twin of Curve25519
with deterministic nonces (a direct defense against the nonce-reuse
catastrophes of ECDSA). EUF-CMA under ECDLP in the random-oracle model. Used
here for ceremony quorum votes (2-of-3) and checkpoints where small,
fast signatures dominate.

AES-256-GCM. 256-bit keys, 96-bit nonces, 128-bit tags. The AEAD bound: forgery
advantage ≈ `q²/2^128` for `q` blocks under one key — the system therefore
rekeys (ratchets) long before approaching dangerous volumes, and every nonce
is used once (counters, never random). Hardware acceleration (AES-NI) is used
where present; the constant-time software path avoids cache-timing leaks.

ChaCha20-Poly1305. 256-bit keys, 96-bit nonces, the AEAD of the TLS 1.3 data
plane and framing layer. ARX design (add-rotate-xor): constant-time by
construction on every platform, no lookup tables, hence the default where
AES hardware is absent.

SHA-3 (Keccak). Sponge construction with capacity `2·output` (e.g., 512-bit
capacity for SHA3-256): collision resistance ≈ 2^128, preimage ≈ 2^256. Used
for checksums (file chunks, transcripts), fingerprints, and KDF extraction.
The sponge indifferentiability result means SHA-3 behaves like a random
oracle up to the capacity bound — the formal basis for using one primitive
across checksums, commitments, and key derivation with domain separation.

HKDF (RFC 5869, with SHA-384 and SHA3-512 instantiations here).
Extract-then-expand: `PRK = HMAC(salt, IKM)`, then `OKM = HMAC-chain(PRK,
info, length)`. The `info` labels are the domain separation that makes every
ratchet output, exporter subkey, and schedule key an independent key —
compromise of one derived key provably (in the PRF model) reveals nothing
about siblings. The live HKDF-SHA384 known-vector gate pins this exactly.

## 2.7 The hybrid combiner (PQXDH v2 shape)

Given shared secrets `s1 (X25519)`, `s2 (ML-KEM)`, `s3 (McEliece)`, the
combiner outputs `K = HKDF-SHA384(salt, s1 ‖ s2 ‖ s3, info, 32+)` with a
fixed purpose label. Lemma (dual-PRF / nested-PRF combiner, standard): if
HKDF is a dual PRF and AT LEAST ONE input is uniformly random and independent
of the adversary's view, then `K` is pseudorandom. Proof sketch: fix all other
inputs as known constants absorbed into the PRF key schedule; the combiner
reduces to a single-key PRF keyed (in the dual sense) by the strong input.
Consequence: the handshake is secure against classical adversaries (X25519
leg), against quantum adversaries if ML-KEM holds, and against lattice-break
adversaries if McEliece holds — simultaneously, with no negotiation downgrade
(the suite is pinned, never negotiated; cf. Volume A downgrade-defense).


## 2.8 Double Ratchet: forward secrecy and post-compromise security

State. Each party holds a root key `RK`, sending/receiving chain keys
`CKs/CKr`, and ratchet key pairs. Two step types: (a) symmetric-chain step —
`CK, MK = KDF(CK, const)`; message key `MK` encrypts one message, `CK`
advances; old chain keys are wiped; (b) DH-ratchet step — on receiving a new
peer ratchet public key, perform the hybrid KEM/DH, mix into `RK`, and start
fresh chains.

Lemma 1 (forward secrecy). Deleting each chain key right after use means a
later compromise reveals nothing about earlier messages: earlier keys are gone
and the KDF is one-way. Formally, the adversary's view after compromise is
independent of pre-compromise chain keys (they were uniform and erased).

Lemma 2 (post-compromise security / healing). One honest DH-ratchet step
after a compromise restores secrecy: the fresh ephemeral KEM randomness is
unknown to the adversary, so the new `RK` (hence all downstream keys) is
pseudorandom to it — provided the adversary is passive during that step (an
active adversary that suppresses the healing message prevents healing; this
is inherent to all messengers and is why the system surfaces rekey
confirmations).

SPQR/Braid-lite parameters used here (gated): 50-message and 7-day rotation
bounds force fresh ratchet steps even on quiet channels, so staleness cannot
accumulate. Break-in recovery events are logged, not silent.

## 2.9 Group key schedule (chained epochs)

Each epoch `e` has an epoch secret `ES_e`. The schedule is a hash chain:
`ES_{e+1} = KDF(ES_e, commit_secret, transcript_hash_e, "epoch")`, where the
commit secret comes from the TreeKEM update path and the transcript hash binds
the entire history (next section). Properties: (a) forward secrecy across
epochs — `ES_e` is wiped on advance; (b) backward isolation — a removed member
who knew `ES_e` cannot compute `ES_{e+1}` without the fresh commit secret,
which is encrypted only to current members' update-path keys; (c) key
independence — distinct epochs' keys are unrelated outputs of the KDF.
The group exporter (§2.11 of this Part is §8.5-analogue in Volume A) derives
application subkeys from `ES_e` with distinct labels, so file transfer,
announcements, and future sub-protocols never share key bytes.

## 2.10 TreeKEM structure layer (resolution, covers, tree hash)

The ratchet tree is a left-balanced binary tree; leaves are members (with
blank slots for removed members). For a committer at leaf `i`, the *direct
path* is the nodes from `i`'s leaf to the root; the *copath* is the siblings
of direct-path nodes; a node's *resolution* is itself if non-blank, else the
resolutions of its children (filtered resolution drops blanks). The committer
samples fresh path secrets, encrypts each to the resolution of the
corresponding copath node, and everyone merges: members on the direct path
get the secret directly, others decrypt via their copath coverage. The
*tree hash* commits to the whole public tree state (member keys, blanks,
parent hashes) so every member verifies the same tree — a forked tree is
detected as a hash mismatch, fail-closed.

Lemma (cover correctness). Every current member belongs to the resolution of
exactly the copath node(s) it needs: by induction on tree height — the
committer's leaf is covered trivially, and each level's sibling subtree is
covered by its resolution by the induction hypothesis; blanks resolve to
their non-blank descendants, so removed members (blanked) are never in any
resolution and receive nothing. This is the structural half of post-compromise
security for groups; the cryptographic half is that each path secret is
fresh and KEM-encrypted (here via the persistent PQ TreeKEM engine).

## 2.11 Transcript binding and fork detection

The transcript hash chains every membership-affecting event:
`T_{e+1} = H(T_e ‖ commit_content_e ‖ suite_annotation_e)`. The suite
annotation is transcript-bound (Volume A §4 framing v2), so a downgrade
attempt changes the transcript and is detected. Fork lemma: two honest
members that accept different histories necessarily hold different transcript
hashes (collision resistance of the hash chain — a fork without detection
would exhibit an explicit SHA-3 collision). The implementation compares
transcript hashes on every commit receive and halts the epoch on mismatch.

## 2.12 BFT quorum mathematics (safety and liveness)

Setup: `N` replicas, at most `f` Byzantine, with `N ≥ 3f + 1` (equivalently
the manager enforces `M ≥ 2f + 1` quorum out of `N`, `M ≥ 2`, `M ≤ N`).
Quorum intersection lemma: any two quorums of size `2f + 1` out of `3f + 1`
intersect in at least `f + 1` replicas, hence at least one honest replica —
so two conflicting decisions cannot both gather a quorum (safety), because
the honest replica in the intersection never votes twice (equivocation
evidence slashes double-voters; the implementation records it forensically).
Liveness sketch (HotStuff-2 shape): with a correct leader and partial
synchrony, two phases (prepare/commit with quorum certificates, offline QC
assembly permitted) drive each view to decision; view-change rotates the
leader so a faulty leader can delay but not deadlock (multi-round ballots in
the manager). Roster caps and vote-stripping bound the adversary's ability to
amplify faulty weight.

## 2.13 Threshold, sharing, Merkle chains, TUF rollback

Shamir 2-of-3 (ceremony quorum): secret `S` with random `a`, shares
`(i, S + a·i)`; any 2 shares interpolate `S`, any 1 share is uniform and
reveals nothing (one equation, two unknowns). Votes are Ed25519 signatures so
each share-holder's assent is individually verifiable.

Merkle chains (audit log, ceremony transcript): each record commits to the
previous record's hash; tampering with record `k` changes every subsequent
hash (induction from collision resistance), so an auditor re-checking the
head verifies the whole chain. WORM triggers + WAL are the storage half;
the hash chain is the cryptographic half.

TUF rollback argument: with 4 roles, dual ML-DSA-87 release signatures, and
monotonic version metadata, a rollback attacker must either forge a
dual-signed older release (break ML-DSA) or present stale metadata whose
version is lower than already seen — rejected by the monotonicity check. The
anti-rollback guarantee is therefore exactly as strong as (signature
unforgeability) AND (client correctly remembers the highest seen version),
which is why the version state lives in tamper-evident storage, not in a
plain file.

## 2.14 What is proven, what is tested, what is neither (read this)

- PROVEN (by others, standard results, sketched above): IND-CCA2 of the KEMs
  under Module-LWE / syndrome-decoding hardness; EUF-CMA of the signatures
  under Module-LWE+SIS / hash properties; AEAD bounds; HKDF domain
  separation; Shamir secrecy; quorum intersection; Merkle binding.
- TESTED LIVE (by this repo's gates, executable): every parameter size in
  §§2.2–2.6 (roundtrips + KATs); combiner outputs; ratchet rotation bounds;
  TreeKEM invariants under seeded fuzz; transcript mismatch halting; quorum
  bound enforcement (`M ≥ 2f+1` etc.); strict validator rejection; traversal
  confinement; fail-closed aborts. These are machine-checked facts about the
  running code, rerunnable with one command (Volume A §9.2).
- NEITHER: no novel theorem about this codebase is claimed; formal
  verification covers the Rust data-plane models only (Kani checks, Volume A
  §9); side-channel resistance beyond constant-time discipline and hardware
  notes isops-assessed, not proven; hardware, facility, and human-procedure
  claims are out of scope for code (Volume A §10).

# VOLUME C, Part 4 — Wire Format Catalog

> Each format is labeled VERIFIED (read directly in this audit) or PRIOR (recorded
> in earlier audited waves with gates). Field orders below are byte orders on the wire.

## 4.1 Group framing v2 envelope — VERIFIED

- `VERSION = 2`. Message kinds include `KIND_UPDATE = 3` (member key update).
- Suite registry: `SUITE_PQ_PURE_1024` is the pinned production suite; hybrid
  suite identifiers exist but are documented-unsupported (downgrade defense: the
  suite is pinned per group, never negotiated).
- Suite annotation: `encode_suite_annotation` / `decode_suite_annotation`
  roundtrip the suite identifier; the annotation is bound into the transcript
  (`extra` transcript input), so altering it forks the transcript detectably.
- KeyPackage lifetime: `not_before` / `not_after` timestamps with `is_live()`
  liveness check; expired or not-yet-valid packages are refused fail-closed.
- Member identifiers: maximum length `MEMBER_ID_MAX_LEN = 256`; longer
  identifiers are rejected at parse (oversize fuzz gate).

## 4.2 File metadata wire layout — VERIFIED

`FileMetadata.to_bytes()` serializes, in order: file_id (32 bytes) +
filename_len (2 bytes) + filename + file_size (8 bytes) + file_type_len
(2 bytes) + file_type + checksum (64 bytes) + chunk_size (4 bytes) +
total_chunks (4 bytes) + timestamp (8 bytes) + sender_id_len (2 bytes) +
sender_id. Validation on construct (`__post_init__`): file_id exactly 32 hex
chars; filename 1–255 chars; file_size 1 byte–1 GB; chunk_size within
(`MIN_CHUNK_SIZE`..1 MB); total_chunks positive. Malformed inputs are rejected
by the parser fuzz gates (truncation, bitflip, garbage, oversize).

## 4.3 Chunk wire rules — VERIFIED

`FileChunk` fields: file_id (32 hex chars), chunk_number (0-based,
non-negative), chunk_data (non-empty, ≤1 MB), chunk_checksum (SHA3-256 hex of
exactly chunk_data, compared with constant-time `hmac.compare_digest`),
is_final flag, optional keyed auth_tag (HMAC-SHA512, origin authentication).
`FileMessage.MIN_CHUNK_SIZE = 4096` (4 KB): smaller chunks are refused because
tiny chunks amplify chunk-table memory (denial-of-service bound). Reassembly
requires a gapless 0-based sequence, then verifies the whole-file SHA3-256
beforeaccepting; mismatch deletes the output and raises fail-closed.

## 4.4 Handshake bundle shape — PRIOR (measured)

The pre-authentication hybrid bundle (X25519 + ML-KEM-1024 + McEliece-8192128f
public keys plus ML-DSA/SLH-DSA signatures) measures ~1.8 MB on the wire
(1,817,211 bytes observed), dominated by the 1,357,824-byte McEliece public
key. Consequence documented in the audit: full bundles cannot traverse
9.6–64 kbps HF/VHF/SATCOM; those links require pre-distributed keys
(out-of-band provisioning). The 2 MB bundle exception exists at exactly the
receive sites that must accept it; every other pre-auth frame keeps the
64 KB cap with the rate limiter concurrent.

## 4.5 Group exporter interface — PRIOR

`export_subkey` derives purpose-bound subkeys from the epoch secret with
HKDF-SHA3-512 and distinct labels per purpose, so file transfer,
announcements, and future sub-protocols never share key bytes (MLS exporter
analogue, RFC 9420 §8.5 shape). Commit signatures (`commit_sig`) authenticate
each epoch transition; Welcome messages carry new members' joining material
with tree-hash confirmation.

# VOLUME C, Part 7 — Operator Manual (non-technical)

> Written for the authorized operator who is not a cryptographer. Every
> procedure here maps to executable gates or code paths documented in Volumes
> A–C. Anything requiring people, buildings, or signatures is marked HUMAN —
> code cannot do it for you.

## 7.1 What this system is, in plain language

Two (or a group of) computers talk directly to each other — no central server
that can read, redirect, or log the conversation. Before any message moves,
the stations perform a handshake that mixes three independent mathematical
locks (one classical, two post-quantum from different families). Every message
after that uses fresh keys that are deleted immediately after use, so stealing
a device later does not unlock old messages (forward secrecy), and the devices
re-lock themselves continuously (healing). Group chats add shared epochs with
the same properties. A strategic layer lets designated stations vote on orders
so no single compromised station can issue them alone. Everything that happens
is written to a tamper-evident audit log.

## 7.2 What this system is not

- Not certified, accredited, or authorized to carry any classified or
  controlled information by anything in this repository. Authorization comes
  only from your Authorizing Official (HUMAN), certification only from the
  designated laboratories (HUMAN).
- Not a replacement for physical security: it cannot detect someone standing
  behind the operator, a camera over the keyboard, or a modified computer.
- Not quantum-proof in any absolute sense: it is resistant under stated,
  published hardness assumptions (Part 2). If those assumptions fall, the
  audit log tells you exactly what was recorded under them.

## 7.3 Installation (lab)

1. Install Python 3.14 and Rust (for the data plane), plus project
   dependencies. Place the provided `oqs.dll` (post-quantum library) and
   `libsodium.dll` beside the application — startup verifies the library's
   signature and refuses to run if it fails (you will see the refusal in the
   log; do not bypass it).
2. Run the deployment verifier: `python verify_deployment.py`. Ship nothing
   unless it reports `READY FOR DEPLOYMENT` with `FAIL: 0`.
3. Run the test suite as the acceptance check. Note: on heavily loaded
   machines the runner itself can die at the very end after all tests pass
   (teardown crash, environmental); judge by the absence of any FAILED lines
   and the per-segment summaries, as documented in Volume A §9.

## 7.4 Configuration flags

All behavior switches are environment variables, fully enumerated in Part 5
of this volume. Rules of thumb: `P2P_PRODUCTION=1` / `SECURE_P2P_PRODUCTION=1`
enable production strictness; `P2P_FAIL_ON_SOFTWARE_FALLBACK=1` makes missing
hardware a hard stop instead of a warning; any flag with LOOPBACK, LAB, or
TEST in its name is lab-only and must never be set on operational machines.
When in doubt, set nothing: defaults fail closed.

## 7.5 Key ceremony operations (HUMAN + tool)

Root authority never belongs to one person: the ceremony tool requires 2 of 3
custodians to sign with independent Ed25519 keys before root material
activates. Procedure: three custodians meet, each on their own machine; two
must approve; the audit log records all three identities and both signatures.
Refused states (only one approval, expired package, mismatched transcript)
halt — that halt is the security working, not a malfunction. Escalate halts
to the security officer; never work around them with flags.

## 7.6 Daily operations

- Start a station with an ephemeral identity for sensitive sessions (keys live
  in locked RAM and are wiped on exit; nothing is stored on disk).
- Join groups only via signed Welcome material; verify the member list after
  joining — a member you did not approve is a compromise until proven otherwise.
- Files received from peers always land inside `downloads/` under neutralized
  names; dotfiles are renamed; anything refused arrives as an explicit error
  message, never silently.
- Watch the audit log, not just the chat window: refused handshakes, failed
  certificate checks, and quarantine holds are recorded there with reasons.

## 7.7 Incident response (plain order)

1. Suspected compromise of a station: remove it from the group (epoch advance
   locks it out cryptographically), then revoke its credentials at the CA.
2. Suspected tamper with a device: trigger the emergency wipe path (keys and
   buffers overwritten before process exit) and treat all material from that
   device as suspect until the audit chain is reviewed.
3. Suspected forged order: check the quorum record — a valid strategic order
   carries a quorum certificate your station verified; an order without one
   was never valid, regardless of what any screen displayed.
4. After any incident: export the audit log first (it is hash-chained; gaps
   are themselves evidence), then rebuild the station from known-good media.

## 7.8 Glossary (short)

- Handshake: the initial lock-mixing both stations perform before talking.
- Ratchet: the continuous re-locking of message keys (forward secrecy + healing).
- Epoch: one generation of group keys; membership changes start a new one.
- Transcript: the running hash-chained history every member independently keeps.
- Quorum: the minimum votes (more than two-thirds) that make an order valid.
- Fail closed: when in doubt, stop and refuse — the system's default.
- KAT (Known-Answer Test): a test that pins a cryptographic output to its
  published standard value; the reason parameter tables in this document can
  be trusted.
